name: Shoulder Crunch Control
description: Lock the opponent's shoulder and head together using the Shoulder Crunch position to set up sweeps, Triangles, Armbars, and Leg Lock entries.
shortInstruction: Pull their head to their shoulder, lock the crunch, attack the exposed side.
summary: The Shoulder Crunch is one of the highest-control positions in no-gi Guard work. By pulling the opponent's head down toward their same-side shoulder (creating a 'crunch' on their neck and shoulder), you limit their movement on that side and expose their far arm, their back, and their legs. The Shoulder Crunch is not a submission itself, it is a control position that makes every attack from Guard easier.
whyItWorks: Pulling their head to their shoulder traps their arm and neck on the same side, limiting their defensive options.
The crunch creates a structural weakness, they cannot posture, frame, or base on the crunched side.
It opens multiple attack lines: Triangle (over the crunched arm), sweep (to the open side), or Leg Lock entry.
Danaher/John Danaher principle: a compromised upper body makes the lower body vulnerable.
commonMistakes: Letting them posture out of the crunch, the crunch requires constant tension.
Pulling their head straight down instead of to the side, the crunch is about the angle, not the depth.
Releasing the crunch to chase a submission, maintain the crunch, and the submission comes to you.
Forgetting to control their free arm, they will use it to post and escape.
coachingCues: Head to shoulder, lock the angle.
The crunch is the cage, the submission is the reward.
Control the free arm, own the position.
If they fight the crunch, they open the Triangle.
safetySummary: Do not crank the opponent's neck, the Shoulder Crunch applies pressure to the shoulder girdle, not the cervical spine.
Release the crunch immediately if your partner taps, neck and shoulder injuries are serious.
Be careful when training with partners who have pre-existing neck or shoulder issues.
keyCorrections: If they posture out, you lost the angle, pull their head back down to their shoulder, not to your chest.
If they square back up, the crunch is too loose, tighten your grip and pull their elbow across their body.
If they attack your legs while you're in the crunch, your legs are too exposed, keep your knees between you and them.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Secure the Shoulder Crunch (head to their shoulder) → control their free arm → attack based on their reaction.

decisionTree.action: Triangle Choke. Option 2: They turn away → sweep or Back Take.
Armbar on the free arm. Option 4: They stand → Leg Lock entry.

moneyDetails: Pull their head to their shoulder, not to your chest, the angle of the crunch is what immobilizes them.
Use your same-side hand to grab their triceps or sleeve on the free arm, this prevents them from posting.
Keep your legs active: one leg on their hip, the other ready to attack the Triangle or sweep.
The Shoulder Crunch is most effective from Butterfly Guard or Half Guard, positions where you are already close to their upper body.
nextStep: After Shoulder Crunch Control, learn the Triangle from Shoulder Crunch and the sweep combinations.
fixItFast: They keep posturing? Pull harder to the side, not down, the lateral pull is harder to resist.
They trap your leg? Your legs are too wide, keep your knees together close to their body.
They grab your free hand? Switch to a collar tie or head control instead.
